hook.text: A cat video hits 50 million views. A health alert reaches billions. Both called 'viral.' Not the same.

buildup.text: True virality means exponential spread—each sharer reaches many, who each reach many more.

discovery.text: Most 'viral' content is actually broadcast—pushed by algorithms to millions from one source.

twist.text: A celebrity's post reaching ten million isn't viral. It's broadcasting. Viral needs chains of strangers.

climax.text: True viral content spreads without platform help. Remove the algorithm and it still moves.

punchline.text: Viral means the audience built itself.

quiz.question: What distinguishes truly viral content from broadcast content?
options: Exponential spread through chains of strangers

hook.text: Hush Puppies shoes were dead in 1994. By 1996, every hip kid in New York wore them. What happened?

buildup.text: Malcolm Gladwell called it the tipping point—the moment a small trend explodes into a phenomenon.

discovery.text: Three factors matter: connectors who know everyone, mavens who know everything, and salesmen who persuade.

twist.text: Critics argue Gladwell oversimplified. Duncan Watts showed random people can trigger tipping points too.

climax.text: The truth is messier. Virality needs the right content in the right network at the right moment.

punchline.text: Everything tips. Predicting when is the hard part.

quiz.question: Who popularized the concept of 'the tipping point'?

hook.text: COVID had an R0 of 2–3: each infected person spread it to two or three others. Content works the same.

buildup.text: In epidemiology, R0 measures spread rate. If R0 exceeds 1, the virus grows. Below 1, it dies.

discovery.text: Content has its own R0. If each viewer causes more than one share on average, the post goes viral.

twist.text: Most content has an R0 near zero. You see it, feel nothing, and scroll past. No spread at all.

climax.text: Viral hits often have R0 above 2. The Ice Bucket Challenge peaked at an estimated R0 of 3.5.

punchline.text: Below one, it dies. Above one, it spreads.

quiz.question: What does an R0 above 1 mean for content?
options: Each viewer generates more than one new share

hook.text: Hotmail added one line to every email: 'Get your free email at Hotmail.' It grew to 12 million users.

buildup.text: The viral coefficient (K) = invites sent × conversion rate. If K > 1, growth is self-sustaining.

discovery.text: Hotmail's K was above 1. Every new user brought in more than one additional user through their emails.

twist.text: Most products have a K far below 1. They need paid marketing to grow. True virality is extremely rare.

climax.text: WhatsApp achieved K > 1 by being better when friends joined. The product improved with each invite.

punchline.text: The best growth engine is the product itself.

quiz.question: What did Hotmail add to every outgoing email to grow virally?

hook.text: Psy's Gangnam Style hit two billion views. His next video? Nobody remembers. Virality rarely repeats.

buildup.text: Most viral creators never go viral again. The conditions are too chaotic to replicate reliably.

discovery.text: Researchers found that prior viral success doesn't predict future virality. Each hit is independent.

twist.text: One exception: accounts that build communities retain attention. Virality fades; loyalty stays.

climax.text: The smartest viral creators convert one-time viewers into subscribers. They trade fame for community.

punchline.text: Going viral is lightning. Community is electricity.

quiz.question: What typically happens to creators after one viral hit?

hook.text: You share a clever article not because it's useful—but because sharing it makes you look smart.

buildup.text: Jonah Berger calls this social currency. We share things that make us appear knowledgeable or cool.

discovery.text: Secret menus, insider knowledge, exclusive access—these spread because possessing them signals status.

twist.text: Social currency explains why false but surprising 'facts' spread faster than boring truths.

climax.text: People don't share information. They share identity. Every post says: 'This is who I am.'

punchline.text: You don't share for them. You share for you.

quiz.question: What is 'social currency' in sharing behavior?
options: Sharing content that makes you look good

hook.text: Calm articles get read. Angry articles get shared. The difference is arousal—your body's activation.

buildup.text: Berger and Milkman studied 7,000 New York Times articles. High-arousal content shared far more.

discovery.text: Awe, anger, and anxiety all drive sharing. They activate the body. Sadness and calm do not.

twist.text: This means uplifting and infuriating content compete for the same viral slot. Both are high-arousal.

climax.text: Platforms discovered this accidentally. But once they knew, they optimized feeds for arousal.

punchline.text: If it gets your heart racing, you'll share it.

quiz.question: Which emotions drive the most sharing according to research?

hook.text: A vegan shares an animal rights article. A libertarian shares a tax meme. Both are signaling identity.

buildup.text: Sharing isn't about information transfer. It's about tribal membership. 'I belong to this group.'

discovery.text: Researchers found people share political news even when they haven't read it. The headline is enough.

twist.text: This means misinformation spreads via identity. Correcting facts doesn't work when sharing is tribal.

climax.text: Platforms amplify identity content because it generates fierce engagement—likes from allies, fights from foes.

punchline.text: You share what you are, not what you know.

quiz.question: Why do people often share political news without reading it?

hook.text: A polished brand post gets ignored. A CEO trips on camera and goes viral. Imperfection sells.

buildup.text: The pratfall effect: competent people become more likeable after a small mistake. It signals humanity.

discovery.text: Psychologist Elliot Aronson proved this in 1966. The expert who spilled coffee was rated most likeable.

twist.text: Brands learned this. 'Authentic' content—raw, messy, unfiltered—outperforms polished production.

climax.text: But manufactured imperfection backfires. Audiences detect staged vulnerability instantly now.

punchline.text: Be real or be ignored. There's no middle.

quiz.question: What is the pratfall effect?
options: Mistakes make competent people more likeable

hook.text: Everyone's talking about a show you haven't watched. You feel anxious, left out, behind. That's FOMO.

buildup.text: Fear of missing out drives sharing because participating in trends is a social survival mechanism.

discovery.text: Scarcity amplifies FOMO. Limited drops, expiring stories, countdown timers—all trigger urgent sharing.

twist.text: FOMO is ancient. Humans evolved to monitor group activities. Missing a feast meant starving alone.

climax.text: Platforms weaponize FOMO with ephemeral content. Stories vanish in 24 hours—share now or lose it.

punchline.text: If you can miss it, you must share it.

quiz.question: Why do disappearing stories drive more sharing?
options: Scarcity triggers FOMO and urgent sharing

hook.text: In 1976, a biologist invented the word 'meme.' He meant cultural genes—ideas that replicate like DNA.

buildup.text: Richard Dawkins argued in The Selfish Gene that ideas evolve through variation, competition, and selection.

discovery.text: A catchy tune, a fashion trend, a slogan—all memes. They spread from brain to brain like viruses.

twist.text: Dawkins never imagined internet memes. He coined the term for cultural evolution, not cat pictures.

climax.text: Yet internet memes follow his rules perfectly. They mutate, compete, and the fittest survive.

punchline.text: Dawkins created a meme about memes.

quiz.question: Who coined the term 'meme'?

hook.text: The same Drake meme has been reused millions of times with different text. The template survives.

buildup.text: Internet memes follow evolutionary rules: they mutate with each share, and only the funniest survive.

discovery.text: Limor Shifman studied meme evolution and found three traits: simplicity, humor, and easy remixability.

twist.text: The most viral memes are never the original. They're the best remix—iteration beats invention.

climax.text: Meme culture mirrors natural selection. Bad mutations die instantly. Good ones spread in hours.

punchline.text: The fittest meme survives. Darwin would approve.

quiz.question: What three traits make memes spread according to Limor Shifman?

hook.text: Distracted Boyfriend. Woman Yelling at Cat. Two Buttons. You know them instantly. Templates are languages.

buildup.text: A meme template provides structure. Users supply the meaning. The format stays; the content changes.

discovery.text: Templates reduce creative friction. You don't need an idea from scratch—just a clever fill-in.

twist.text: The simplest templates spread furthest. Complex formats limit participation. Memes are democratic art.

climax.text: Templates now shape political discourse. Policy debates happen through meme formats, not essays.

punchline.text: The format is the message.

quiz.question: Why do simpler meme templates spread further?
options: They reduce creative friction and invite more participation

hook.text: In 2016, Pepe the Frog became a hate symbol. A harmless cartoon weaponized through meme culture.

buildup.text: Political operators discovered memes bypass critical thinking. You laugh first, analyze never.

discovery.text: Russia's Internet Research Agency mass-produced memes targeting U.S. voters. Cheap, effective, deniable.

twist.text: Both sides use memes now. The format is neutral—it amplifies whatever message fits the template.

climax.text: Memes are hard to regulate. They're satire, parody, and propaganda simultaneously. The law can't keep up.

punchline.text: A joke can do what a speech cannot.

quiz.question: Why are memes effective as political tools?
options: They bypass critical thinking through humor

hook.text: A meme peaks on Monday. By Friday, your boss uses it. By Sunday, it's dead. Overuse kills memes.

buildup.text: Every meme has a lifecycle: niche creation, mass adoption, corporate co-option, and death.

discovery.text: Brands kill memes fastest. When a meme appears in an ad, its coolness evaporates instantly.

twist.text: Some memes resist death through ironic reuse. Using a 'dead' meme becomes its own meta-joke.

climax.text: Meme culture accelerates. What once lasted months now burns through its lifecycle in days.

punchline.text: The internet creates and kills at the same speed.

quiz.question: What typically kills a meme fastest?

hook.text: A phone network with one user is useless. With two, it has one connection. With ten, it has 45.

buildup.text: Metcalfe's Law: a network's value grows with the square of its users. Doubling users quadruples value.

discovery.text: This explains why social platforms grow explosively. Each new user makes the network better for all.

twist.text: It also explains lock-in. Leaving Facebook means losing your connections. The network owns you.

climax.text: Critics say Metcalfe overestimates. Not all connections are equal. Your thousandth friend adds little.

punchline.text: The network's value isn't in the product. It's in you.

quiz.question: According to Metcalfe's Law, how does network value grow?

hook.text: Your close friends know the same people you do. Your acquaintances know entirely different worlds.

buildup.text: Mark Granovetter's 1973 paper proved that weak ties—casual acquaintances—are bridges between clusters.

discovery.text: Most job referrals come through weak ties. Most viral content spreads through weak ties too.

twist.text: Social media massively increased weak ties. You're connected to thousands you barely know—ideal for virality.

climax.text: Strong ties share deeply. Weak ties share widely. For virality, breadth beats depth every time.

punchline.text: Acquaintances spread more than friends do.

quiz.question: Why are weak ties important for viral spread?

hook.text: One percent of Twitter users produce 80% of all tweets. A tiny minority dominates the conversation.

buildup.text: In epidemiology, super-spreaders infect far more than average. Social networks have them too.

discovery.text: Super-spreaders aren't always famous. Some are just hyper-connected individuals at network crossroads.

twist.text: Targeting super-spreaders is more effective than mass campaigns. One right person beats a million wrong ones.

climax.text: Disinformation campaigns exploit this. Infect a super-spreader with a lie and the network carries it.

punchline.text: One node can move an entire network.

quiz.question: What makes someone a social media super-spreader?

hook.text: A teenager shares K-pop in a gaming forum. Two unrelated communities collide. The meme explodes.

buildup.text: Bridge nodes exist in multiple communities at once. They carry content across social boundaries.

discovery.text: Content that crosses community boundaries reaches exponentially more people than content staying within one.

twist.text: Most content never crosses. It circulates within its origin community and fades. Bridges are rare and valuable.

climax.text: Brands pay influencers who straddle communities. A beauty guru who also games reaches two audiences.

punchline.text: Virality isn't about loudness. It's about bridges.

quiz.question: What is a 'bridge node' in a social network?

hook.text: Stanley Milgram proved in 1967 that any two Americans are connected by about six handshakes.

buildup.text: Six degrees of separation means information can theoretically reach anyone on Earth in six hops.

discovery.text: Facebook found its users averaged 3.57 degrees of separation. The world shrank since Milgram's era.

twist.text: Fewer degrees means faster spread. A rumor can reach billions in hours—far faster than any broadcast.

climax.text: The small world effect makes both good ideas and dangerous lies spread at the same terrifying speed.

punchline.text: The world got smaller. That's not always good.

quiz.question: What did Facebook find about degrees of separation among its users?

hook.text: A false claim about vaccines reached 100 million people before fact-checkers even noticed it existed.

buildup.text: MIT found falsehoods spread six times faster than truth on Twitter. Lies are novel; truth is boring.

discovery.text: False news triggers surprise and disgust—high-arousal emotions that drive sharing. Truth triggers nothing.

twist.text: Corrections travel ten times slower than the original lie. By the time truth arrives, belief is set.

climax.text: The 'illusory truth effect' means repeated lies feel true. Viral repetition becomes belief.

punchline.text: A lie shared enough times becomes the truth.

quiz.question: Why does false news spread faster than truth?

hook.text: Justine Sacco tweeted a bad joke to 170 followers. She landed 11 hours later to worldwide condemnation.

buildup.text: While she flew, the tweet went viral. Strangers tracked her flight. A hashtag trended. Her career ended.

discovery.text: Jon Ronson studied viral shaming. The punishment never fits the crime. One mistake becomes a life sentence.

twist.text: Participants feel righteous. Each person adds one small push. Nobody thinks they're part of a mob.

climax.text: Viral justice has no appeals court. No proportionality. No forgiveness mechanism. Only the pile-on.

punchline.text: The mob doesn't punish. It destroys.

quiz.question: What happened to Justine Sacco after her tweet went viral?
options: Her career was destroyed by worldwide condemnation

hook.text: Barbra Streisand sued to remove a photo of her house. Before the suit: six views. After: 420,000.

buildup.text: Trying to suppress information online almost always backfires. Suppression creates curiosity.

discovery.text: The Streisand Effect: attempting to hide something draws more attention to it than ignoring it would.

twist.text: Governments trigger it constantly. Banning a book makes it a bestseller. Censoring a post makes it famous.

climax.text: The internet treats censorship as damage and routes around it—as cyberpunk pioneer John Gilmore said.

punchline.text: Try to hide it and the internet shows everyone.

quiz.question: What is the Streisand Effect?
options: Suppressing information draws more attention to it

hook.text: A food blogger deliberately cooks pasta wrong. Italians rage. Millions of views. She profits from fury.

buildup.text: Rage bait is content designed to anger a specific group. The creator wants hate-engagement, not love.

discovery.text: Algorithms can't tell angry clicks from happy ones. Rage engagement counts the same. Revenue flows.

twist.text: A cottage industry of rage bait emerged. Creators deliberately offend communities for algorithmic reward.

climax.text: Responding to rage bait amplifies it. The only winning move is to not engage—but outrage is addictive.

punchline.text: Your anger is someone else's paycheck.

quiz.question: Why does rage bait succeed economically?
options: Algorithms treat angry engagement the same as positive
Rage bait is cheaper to produce

hook.text: A teenager posts a dance video. It gets mocked. The mockery goes viral. She deletes her account.

buildup.text: Viral shame is uniquely cruel. Before the internet, embarrassment was local and temporary.

discovery.text: Online shame is permanent, searchable, and global. A moment of cringe follows you for years.

twist.text: The shamers forget quickly. The shamed person doesn't. Studies show viral shaming causes lasting trauma.

climax.text: Some victims changed their names. Others withdrew from public life entirely. Digital shame is exile.

punchline.text: The internet remembers what you wish it would forget.

quiz.question: What makes online shaming different from traditional embarrassment?

hook.text: Why does a $100 cheesesteak go viral but a better restaurant stays unknown? Berger cracked the formula.

buildup.text: STEPPS: Social currency, Triggers, Emotion, Public visibility, Practical value, Stories.

discovery.text: Each element increases sharing probability. Combine several and virality becomes far more likely.

twist.text: But STEPPS isn't a guarantee. You can hit every mark and still fail. The network decides, not the content.

climax.text: Berger found triggers matter most. KitKat paired with coffee breaks—sales surged because coffee is daily.

punchline.text: Great content isn't enough. It needs a trigger.

quiz.question: What does STEPPS stand for in Berger's virality framework?
options: Speed, Timing, Effort, Promotion, Platform, Size
Social currency, Triggers, Emotion, Public, Practical value, Stories
Share, Track, Engage, Post, Promote, Scale

hook.text: You check your phone 96 times a day. Not because you planned to—because apps hooked you.

buildup.text: Nir Eyal's Hook Model: Trigger → Action → Variable reward → Investment. Repeat until habit forms.

discovery.text: The variable reward is key. Slot machines and feeds both use it—you never know what's next.

twist.text: Eyal later wrote a book on breaking these habits. The man who taught companies to addict you recanted.

climax.text: Every major platform follows the Hook Model. The notification is the trigger. The scroll is the reward.

punchline.text: The hook isn't a feature. It's the whole product.

quiz.question: What is the key element that makes the Hook Model addictive?

hook.text: Sean Ellis coined 'growth hacking' in 2010. He meant marketing run by engineers, not Mad Men.

buildup.text: Growth hackers treat user acquisition like a code problem. Run experiments, measure results, iterate.

discovery.text: Airbnb hacked Craigslist—cross-posting listings without permission. Millions of users poured in.

twist.text: Growth hacking blurred ethics. Many tactics exploited dark patterns: tricking users into inviting friends.

climax.text: The era faded as platforms closed loopholes. But the mindset survived. Every startup still thinks in hacks.

punchline.text: Growth hacking isn't marketing. It's engineering luck.

quiz.question: Who coined the term 'growth hacking'?

hook.text: Dropbox offered 250 MB free storage for every friend you invited. The waiting list hit 75,000 overnight.

buildup.text: Traditional ads cost Dropbox $300 per customer. The referral program cost under $1 per signup.

discovery.text: The trick: both sides got rewarded. You got storage, your friend got storage. Everyone wins.

twist.text: Signups increased 60% permanently. Not a spike—a sustained growth engine powered by users themselves.

climax.text: PayPal did it first—literally paying users $10 to sign up and $10 for each referral. Costly but effective.

punchline.text: The cheapest ad is a happy user.

quiz.question: How did Dropbox's referral program drive growth?
options: Giving free storage to both referrer and invitee

hook.text: Netflix spent millions predicting which shows would be hits. They still funded many flops.

buildup.text: Prediction models look at content features, creator history, timing, and network structure.

discovery.text: Duncan Watts proved that success in cultural markets is inherently unpredictable. Randomness dominates.

twist.text: In his Music Lab experiment, the same song could be a hit or a flop. Social influence determined it.

climax.text: You can increase the odds with Berger's STEPPS. But guaranteed virality remains impossible.

punchline.text: You can build the rocket. You can't control the wind.

quiz.question: What did Duncan Watts' Music Lab experiment prove?
options: Success is inherently unpredictable due to social influence
